level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:PATH (@file.path:*/.local/share/kitty/cat.py OR (@file.path:*/.config/systemd/user/* AND @file.path:*.service)) @process.name:(npm OR node OR bun OR yarn OR pnpm OR sh OR bash)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten event_platform=Lin TargetFileName=/(\/\.local\/share\/kitty\/cat\.py|\/\.config\/systemd\/user\/[^\/]+\.service)$/ ContextImageFileName=/(npm|node|bun|yarn|pnpm|sh|bash|dash|zsh)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*/.local/share/kitty/cat.py" OR (Filesystem.file_path="*/.config/systemd/user/*" AND Filesystem.file_path="*.service")) AND Filesystem.process_name IN ("npm","node","bun","yarn","pnpm","npx","sh","bash","dash","zsh") by host, user, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.process, Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*/.local/share/kitty/cat.py" OR (Filesystem.file_path="*/.config/systemd/user/*" AND Filesystem.file_path="*.service")) AND Filesystem.process_name IN ("npm","node","bun","yarn","pnpm","npx","sh","bash","dash","zsh") by host, user, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.process, Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Mini Shai-Hulud C2 backchannel: python polling GitHub commit search for 'firedalazer' AICommand & Control High
Detects Python processes reaching api.github.com/search/commits with the 'firedalazer' keyword — the C2 backchannel used by the kitty/cat.py daemon to fetch RSA-PSS-signed command payloads. Hourly poll cadence and the specific search keyword make this article-grade high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim 'polls the GitHub commit search API hourly for commands containing the keyword firedalazer'. The hourly poll cadence (PollCount >= 4 over 7d window catches the daemon while avoiding a one-off curl), python initiator with cat.py in the cmdline, and the unique 'firedalazer' keyword all combine to article-grade fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal devops automation polling api.github.com via python-requests (rare and easy to allowlist by SourceIP)
  • Security researcher manually querying GitHub search API for firedalazer/Shai-Hulud IOC enumeration (low-volume, single host)
  • CI runner with a custom python script syncing release notes from GitHub
  • Snyk/Socket/StepSecurity research scanners polling for IOC propagation
  • GitHub backup-tool sync jobs running under python that happen to hit /search/commits
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("snyk","socket-cli","stepsecurity","pip install")) | where not (DeviceName has_any ("-research","-redteam","-soc-"))
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — get the Python process tree. Confirm parent is kitty/cat.py or systemd-user. Capture cat.py SHA256 and content. Step 2: Contain — isolate the host. Kill the python process and disable the systemd user unit ('systemctl --user disable --now <unit>'). Block api.github.com at egress only for the affected host (don't blanket-block — GitHub is critical). Treat all secrets accessible to that user account as compromised; rotate them. Step 3: Hunt — pivot to GitHub Audit Log for the user's PAT showing /search/commits queries with 'firedalazer'. Search for repos created under user's account with Dune-themed names (UC6). Check for sibling persistence (.claude UC, .vscode UC).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python.exe","python3","python3.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("cat.py",".local/share/kitty","kitty\\cat.py","firedalazer")
| summarize PollCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| where PollCount >= 4
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName =~ "api.github.com" or RequestURL has "api.github.com"
| where RequestURL has "/search/commits" or RequestURL has "firedalazer"
| where RequestClientApplication startswith "python-requests"
| summarize PollCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            SampleUrls = make_set(RequestURL, 5)
          by SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestClientApplication
| where PollCount >= 4
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\Python.exe OR */python OR */python3) @DestinationHostname:api.github.com @CommandLine:(*cat.py* OR *kitty* OR *firedalazer*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^api\.github\.com$/i ContextImageFileName=/python(3)?(\.exe)?$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(cat\.py|kitty[\\\/]cat\.py|\.local[\\\/]share[\\\/]kitty|firedalazer)/i}, field=ContextProcessId, key=TargetProcessId, include=[CommandLine])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
| _count >= 4
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.dest="api.github.com" AND (Web.url="*search/commits*" OR Web.url="*firedalazer*") AND (Web.http_user_agent="python-requests*") by host, src, src_user, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | stats count min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime dc(url) as distinct_urls values(http_user_agent) as ua by host, src, src_user | where count >= 4
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.dest="api.github.com" AND (Web.url="*search/commits*" OR Web.url="*firedalazer*") AND (Web.http_user_agent="python-requests*") by host, src, src_user, Web.url, Web.http_method, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | stats count min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime dc(url) as distinct_urls values(http_user_agent) as ua by host, src, src_user | where count >= 4
Mini Shai-Hulud GitHub dead-drop exfiltration via python-requests/2.31.0 AIActions on Objectives High
Detects POST/PUT to api.github.com from a python-requests/2.31.0 User-Agent creating Dune-themed repositories or committing 'results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json' files. This is the article's secondary exfil channel activated when the malware harvests a developer's GitHub PAT, used to stash AES-256-GCM-encrypted credential dumps. Rationale: Anchored on the article's three concrete IOCs: User-Agent string 'python-requests/2.31.0', the exfil filename pattern 'results/results-<timestamp>-<counter>.json', and the Dune-themed repo naming convention (sardaukar/fremen/atreides + sandworm/ornithopter/stillsuit). Triple-anchor (UA + method + path keyword) keeps FP rate well below a generic python-requests-to-github hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1567 T1102.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal Python tooling that legitimately creates GitHub repos via PyGithub or python-requests (rare; usually uses official PyGithub UA)
  • CI/CD pipelines using python-requests to push release artifacts to GitHub releases
  • Security tools (Snyk, Socket, dependency-track) authenticating to api.github.com with python-requests
  • Internal automation pinned to python-requests/2.31.0 — coincidental UA collision (rotate to specific UA strings if hits are noisy)
  • Dune-themed-naming-convention coincidence in a legitimate internal repo (extremely unlikely combined with UA + POST + python-requests)
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("PyGithub","snyk","socket-cli")) | where not (SourceIP in ("<ci-runner-cidr>"))
Response runbook
Step 1: Triage — identify the GitHub account whose PAT was used (PAT prefix in proxy auth header if logged, otherwise correlate by SourceIP + SourceUserName). Pull GitHub Audit for repo.create events from that user in the last 7d; flag any matching the Dune keyword regex. Step 2: Contain — revoke the user's GitHub PAT and OAuth tokens via GitHub Enterprise admin. Delete the dead-drop repos. Treat ALL data the developer had on disk as exfiltrated (AWS/GCP/Azure tokens, npm tokens, SSH keys, k8s configs, ~/.netrc). Rotate every credential listed in Stage 4 of the article. Step 3: Hunt — pivot to UC1 (npm→bun) and UC4 (kitty/cat.py) on the same host. Search for hash a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c across the fleet. Check whether any of the user's npm publish tokens were used in the 24h window (npm Audit log) — token may be in the worm-propagation pipeline.
let SuspiciousPython = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ ("python.exe","python","python3.exe","python3")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("cat.py",".local/share/kitty","kitty\\cat.py")
    | project DeviceId, ProcessId, PyStart=Timestamp, PyCmd=ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python","python3.exe","python3")
| join kind=inner SuspiciousPython on DeviceId, $left.InitiatingProcessId == $right.ProcessId
| summarize Connections = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            SampleUrls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 5), SampleCmd = any(PyCmd)
          by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName =~ "api.github.com"
| where RequestClientApplication startswith "python-requests/2.31"
| where RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT","PATCH")
| where RequestURL has_any ("/user/repos","/contents/results-","sardaukar","fremen","atreides","sandworm","ornithopter","stillsuit","harkonnen")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, SentBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mini Shai-Hulud GitHub dead-drop exfiltration (Dune-themed repos via python-requests)
id: 8a1b5c3d-4e7f-4b9c-9a2e-1d6f8c4b3e7a
description: Detects POST/PUT to api.github.com from python-requests/2.31.0 creating Dune-themed dead-drop repos or committing results-<ts>.json — the Mini Shai-Hulud AntV credential-dump exfiltration channel.
references:
  - https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/19
tags:
  - attack.t1567
  - attack.t1102.003
  - attack.exfiltration
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  selection_host:
    cs-host: 'api.github.com'
  selection_ua:
    cs-user-agent|startswith: 'python-requests/2.31'
  selection_method:
    cs-method:
      - 'POST'
      - 'PUT'
      - 'PATCH'
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - '/user/repos'
      - '/contents/results-'
      - 'sardaukar'
      - 'fremen'
      - 'atreides'
      - 'sandworm'
      - 'ornithopter'
      - 'stillsuit'
  condition: selection_host and selection_ua and selection_method and selection_path
level: high
@http.url_details.host:api.github.com @http.useragent:python-requests/2.31.0* @http.method:(POST OR PUT OR PATCH) @http.url:(*/user/repos* OR */contents/results-* OR *sardaukar* OR *fremen* OR *atreides* OR *sandworm* OR *ornithopter* OR *stillsuit*)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/python(3)?(\.exe)?$/i RemotePort=443
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^api\.github\.com$/i}, field=aid, key=aid, include=[DomainName])
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(cat\.py|kitty[\\\/]cat\.py|results-\d+|sardaukar|fremen|atreides|sandworm|ornithopter|stillsuit)/i}, field=ContextProcessId, key=TargetProcessId, include=[CommandLine])

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1204.002

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'

            - 'wget '

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or SHA1 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or MD5 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or SHA1 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or MD5 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Malicious node-ipc package landed on disk under node_modules
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Malicious node-ipc versions published to npm in suspected maintainer account com
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] node-ipc stealer __ntw=1 environment marker in process command line
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS lookup for azurestaticprovider[.]net node-ipc exfil domain · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Outbound egress to node-ipc stealer infrastructure (azurestaticprovider[.]net / 37.16.75.69) · [LLM] node.js process staging credential dump in nt-* temp directory
Outbound egress to node-ipc stealer infrastructure (azurestaticprovider[.]net / 37.16.75.69) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects network connections to attacker-owned exfiltration infrastructure used by the malicious node-ipc 9.1.6 / 9.2.3 / 12.0.1 npm packages published 14 May 2026. Any host reaching these atoms after package install should be treated as a credential-theft incident. Rationale: Pivots on two atomic IOCs explicitly named in the Snyk advisory (37.16.75.69 and azurestaticprovider.net), each independently corroborated by StepSecurity and Upwind. No expected legitimate traffic to either atom — attacker-owned exfil infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.upwind.io/feed/malicious-node-ipc-npm-package-credential-theft • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/stealer-backdoor-found-in-3-node-ipc.html
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Researcher / red-team sandbox intentionally detonating a node-ipc IOC sample
  • Threat-intel platform validating IOC reachability from an enrichment sensor
  • Internal honeypot or canary host instrumented to call known-bad domains for SOC training
  • DNS-over-HTTPS resolver logs caching previous lookups when no real connection was made
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonator","sentinel-ti-","honeypot") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("thor.exe","loki.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): On any hit, immediately enumerate the initiating process tree (InitiatingProcessFileName + parent) — confirm whether the originating process is node.exe / node and which package directory was loaded. Pull `npm ls node-ipc` and lockfile contents from the host. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the device, block 37.16.75.69 and *.azurestaticprovider.net at egress, kill the offending node process, and revoke ALL credentials accessible from that environment (npm tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS keys, SSH, kubeconfig, GCP service accounts, Terraform state, shell-history-resident secrets). Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the firing host's outbound connections for the prior 7 days to surface staging/recon connections; sweep CI runners and developer laptops for the affected node-ipc versions and for the related UCs (DNS lookups, __ntw=1 marker, nt-* temp dirs).
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteIP == "37.16.75.69"
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("azurestaticprovider.net","sh.azurestaticprovider.net")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,

| order by Timestamp desc

    or DestinationHostName has "azurestaticprovider.net"
    or RequestURL has "azurestaticprovider.net"
 | project TimeGenerated, SourceUserName, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct),
(ImNetworkSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DstIpAddr == "37.16.75.69"
    or DstHostname has "azurestaticprovider.net"
    or Url has "azurestaticprovider.net"
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, EventProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outbound Connection to node-ipc Stealer Infrastructure (azurestaticprovider.net)
id: 8b9d2a31-7e54-4d12-9a2b-3c8f1e0b4a76
description: Detects outbound connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure used by the malicious node-ipc 9.1.6 / 9.2.3 / 12.0.1 npm supply-chain payload published on 14 May 2026.
references:
  - https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-node-ipc-versions-published-npm/
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack
  - https://www.upwind.io/feed/malicious-node-ipc-npm-package-credential-theft
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/19
tags:
  - attack.exfiltration
  - attack.t1041
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_ip:
    DestinationIp: '37.16.75.69'
  selection_host:
    DestinationHostname|contains:
      - 'azurestaticprovider.net'
  condition: selection_ip or selection_host
falsepositives:
  - None expected; infrastructure is attacker-owned per StepSecurity, Snyk, Upwind, and Socket analysis
level: high

(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationIp:37.16.75.69 OR @DestinationHostname:(*azurestaticprovider.net* OR *AzureStaticProvider.net*))) OR (source:linux.auditd (@network.destination.ip:37.16.75.69 OR @network.destination.domain:*azurestaticprovider.net*)) OR (source:windows.defender (@FilePath:*azurestaticprovider.net* OR @ThreatName:*node-ipc*))
(#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 OR #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP6 OR #event_simpleName=DnsRequest)
| (RemoteAddressIP4="37.16.75.69" OR RemoteAddressIP6="37.16.75.69" OR DomainName=/azurestaticprovider\.net$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort, DomainName], function=count())
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.app) as app values(All_Traffic.process) as process values(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Network_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="37.16.75.69" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="azurestaticprovider.net" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="sh.azurestaticprovider.net" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*.azurestaticprovider.net") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.app) as app values(All_Traffic.process) as process values(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Network_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="37.16.75.69" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="azurestaticprovider.net" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="sh.azurestaticprovider.net" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*.azurestaticprovider.net") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
DNS lookup for azurestaticprovider[.]net node-ipc exfil domain AICommand & Control High
Surfaces hosts resolving the attacker-controlled domain azurestaticprovider.net (or sh.azurestaticprovider.net) used by the malicious node-ipc payload, even when the subsequent TCP egress is firewall-blocked. DNS-layer pivot catches hosts that loaded the package but did not complete exfiltration. Rationale: DNS pivot catches the same campaign at an earlier layer than TCP egress and survives proxy-level blocks. Domain is unique to this campaign and referenced verbatim in StepSecurity, Upwind, and Snyk advisories. ContextImageFileName lets the analyst confirm node.exe / npm as the requesting process. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.upwind.io/feed/malicious-node-ipc-npm-package-credential-theft
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment sensor doing IOC reachability checks
  • DNS server forwarding cache-warmup queries from another resolver
  • Security researcher / SOC analyst running curl/dig from a jump host
  • RPZ logging shows blocked queries — confirms detection efficacy, not malicious activity
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("ti-enrich-","sandbox-","honeypot-"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the requesting process via ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName — confirm node.exe / npm / yarn / pnpm as parent and pull the host's package-lock.json for node-ipc versions 9.1.6 / 9.2.3 / 12.0.1. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole or RPZ-block *.azurestaticprovider.net at the resolver, isolate any developer/CI host where the lookup originated, rotate all credentials reachable from that environment (npm, GitHub, AWS, SSH, kube, Terraform state, GCP). Step 3 (hunt): Cross-reference against UC1 (TCP egress) to see whether exfiltration completed; if no TCP follow-on the credentials may still be unexposed — but assume compromise. Sweep the org for additional node-ipc installs via npm/yarn/pnpm lockfile inventory.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "azurestaticprovider.net"
   or RemoteUrl endswith ".azurestaticprovider.net"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(),
            SampleProc=any(InitiatingProcessFileName),
            SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
            SampleUser=any(InitiatingProcessAccountName)
            by DeviceName, RemoteUrl
| order by FirstSeen asc
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Name has "azurestaticprovider.net"
 | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode),
(ImDnsActivity
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DnsQuery has "azurestaticprovider.net"
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName, EventProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated asc

node-ipc stealer __ntw=1 environment marker in process command line AIInstallation High
Hunts for the __ntw=1 environment-variable marker reportedly used by the malicious node-ipc payload to signal that a child has already inherited the stealer context (preventing re-entry). Presence of this token in any process or child command-line is a high-fidelity indicator the payload executed on the host. Rationale: `__ntw=1` is a campaign-specific environment marker called out verbatim in the Snyk advisory and corroborated by StepSecurity — no mainstream npm package or build tool uses this token. Single-string match on CommandLine works because env vars set inline (e.g. `__ntw=1 node ...`) and parent-spawned children with that prefix surface in EDR command-line telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.upwind.io/feed/malicious-node-ipc-npm-package-credential-theft
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / IR analyst reproducing the malware on a sandbox
  • Internal threat-hunt query stored in an analyst's shell history that gets re-exec'd
  • Sigma/test harness firing a synthetic event with the literal IOC for tuning
  • Documentation file or README opened in an editor whose telemetry surfaces __ntw=1 in the process arglist of a grep/findstr
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox-","detonator-","malware-rev-") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("grep.exe","findstr.exe","rg.exe","sigma-cli"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full process tree around the hit — parent (likely node.exe / npm / yarn / pnpm), command line, and SHA256. Confirm whether node_modules/node-ipc/node-ipc.cjs exists on the host and what version is recorded in package-lock.json or yarn.lock. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the node process tree, quarantine the affected package directory, and rotate every credential category named in the advisory (npm, GitHub PAT/SSH, AWS / Azure / GCP, kubeconfig, Terraform state, ~/.bash_history-resident secrets, AI/dev-tool API keys). Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts in the org for the same IOC, then pivot to UC1/UC2 (egress + DNS) for the same host's prior 7 days to confirm exfiltration completion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "__ntw=1"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "__ntw=1"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImProcessCreate
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "__ntw=1"
    or ParentProcessCommandLine has "__ntw=1"
    or TargetProcessCommandLine has "__ntw=1"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessCommandLine, EventProduct),
(SecurityEvent
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where EventID == 4688
 | where CommandLine has "__ntw=1" or ParentProcessName has "__ntw=1"
 | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, ProcessId)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious node-ipc package landed on disk under node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for file-system writes of node-ipc.cjs into any node_modules/node-ipc/ directory after the 14 May 2026 publication window, surfacing developer workstations, CI runners, build containers, and artifact registries that installed a candidate-malicious release. Pair with version triage (9.1.6 / 9.2.3 / 12.0.1). Rationale: Anchors on the exact CommonJS file Snyk identifies as malicious (`node-ipc.cjs`) and the canonical install path (`node_modules/node-ipc/`). Time-bound to the publication window so analysts only see installs that could be the bad versions. Hunting tier because a hit alone does not prove the version is malicious — needs package.json/lockfile triage as Step 1. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.upwind.io/feed/malicious-node-ipc-npm-package-credential-theft • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/stealer-backdoor-found-in-3-node-ipc.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer installing a still-uncompromised legacy version (e.g. 12.0.0) after the cutoff
  • CI cache warmup writing node-ipc into a build container from a private mirror with safe versions
  • Docker image layer-extraction surfacing node-ipc.cjs writes from older base images
  • Local node_modules vendoring during yarn/pnpm migrations (massive file-create bursts that include node-ipc)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the sibling `package.json` (`FolderPath/../package.json`) on each host and confirm version. Versions 9.1.6, 9.2.3, 12.0.1 = malicious; anything else = downgrade or pin. Step 2 (contain): On confirmed malicious version — isolate the host, delete the affected node_modules tree, clear the npm/yarn/pnpm cache, refresh the lockfile pinning to a safe version, and treat all credentials accessible from that environment as exposed. Step 3 (hunt): Inventory ALL artifact registries (Artifactory, Nexus, internal npm proxy), CI cache volumes, ephemeral build worker images, and Docker layers for the same file; pivot to UC1/UC2/UC3 on each candidate host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp >= datetime(2026-05-14T00:00:00Z)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "node-ipc.cjs"
| where FolderPath has "node_modules" and FolderPath has "node-ipc"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp asc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated >= datetime(2026-05-14T00:00:00Z)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate")
| where TargetFileName =~ "node-ipc.cjs"
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules" and TargetFilePath has "node-ipc"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated asc
title: Malicious node-ipc CommonJS Bundle Written Under node_modules (May 2026)
id: c41a83d7-2e0b-4f6a-90ef-7d8b1c2a5e09
description: Detects creation/modification of node_modules/node-ipc/node-ipc.cjs after 14 May 2026, the publication date of the malicious 9.1.6, 9.2.3, and 12.0.1 releases.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/19
tags:

logsource:

detection:

level: medium

(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\\node_modules\\node-ipc\\node-ipc.cjs OR @TargetFilename:*/node_modules/node-ipc/node-ipc.cjs)) OR (source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:PATH @file.path:*/node_modules/node-ipc/node-ipc.cjs)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| regex("(/|\\\\)node_modules(/|\\\\)node-ipc(/|\\\\)node-ipc\\.cjs$", field=TargetFileName, flags=i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, UserName], function=min(@timestamp))
| _time >= 1747180800000

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc values(Filesystem.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="node-ipc.cjs" AND Filesystem.file_path="*node_modules*node-ipc*" AND Filesystem.action="created" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where firstTime >= relative_time(now(),"-30d@d") AND firstTime >= strptime("2026-05-14T00:00:00","%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

node.js process staging credential dump in nt-* temp directory AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the staging artefact the malicious node-ipc payload writes — a temp directory matching `$TMPDIR/nt-*` populated by a node process — used to compress harvested SSH / cloud / kube / GitHub / Terraform / shell-history credentials before exfil. Catches the campaign at the collection layer even if egress is firewall-blocked. Rationale: Combines two campaign-specific behaviours from the Snyk advisory: (a) the temp directory prefix `nt-` and (b) a node process as the writer. Threshold of ≥3 distinct files per directory suppresses single-file noise while still firing on the credential-dump fan-out (90+ categories). Catches the campaign at the collection step even when egress is blocked. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.upwind.io/feed/malicious-node-ipc-npm-package-credential-theft
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1552.001 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Node.js test framework (e.g. some Jest/Mocha snapshot tooling) writing nt-prefixed scratch files
  • Node.js native build (node-gyp) using temp scratch directories during compile
  • Electron app's installer/updater extracting nt-prefixed temp artefacts on Windows
  • A developer running a CLI tool whose temp prefix happens to begin with 'nt'
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","electron-builder","jest","mocha") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") and DistinctFiles < 10)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the file inventory inside the matching nt-* directory — confirm presence of files resembling credential artefacts (id_rsa, .aws/credentials, kubeconfig, .gitconfig, .npmrc, .terraformrc, .bash_history). Check the writing process tree for node-ipc on disk. Step 2 (contain): Kill the node process, isolate the host, preserve the nt-* directory for forensics, and rotate every credential the host had access to (treat as fully compromised; the staging dir confirms collection occurred). Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC1/UC2 (azurestaticprovider.net + 37.16.75.69 egress) on the same host to determine whether the stage was exfiltrated; sweep CI runners for the same staging pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)([\\/]Temp[\\/]nt-|/tmp/nt-|/var/folders/.+?/T/nt-)"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp),
            DistinctFiles=dcount(FileName), SampleFiles=make_set(FileName, 25),
            TotalBytes=sum(FileSize)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FolderPath
| where DistinctFiles >= 3
| order by FirstSeen asc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)([\\/]Temp[\\/]nt-|/tmp/nt-|/var/folders/.+?/T/nt-)"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), DistinctFiles=dcount(TargetFileName),
            SampleFiles=make_set(TargetFileName, 25), TotalBytes=sum(TargetFileSize)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, EventProduct
| where DistinctFiles >= 3
| order by FirstSeen asc

FrostyNeighbor PicassoLoader drop to %AppData%\WinDataScope\Update.js AIInstallation High
Hunts the article-specific second-stage drop: a JavaScript PicassoLoader payload written to a fixed AppData subfolder ('WinDataScope') used by FrostyNeighbor's March 2026 Ukrtelecom-themed compromise chain. The folder name and filename are both fingerprinted by ESET against multiple samples in this campaign. Rationale: WinDataScope is a folder name nowhere referenced in legitimate software inventories — ESET fingerprints it directly to FrostyNeighbor's PicassoLoader staging in the May 2026 report. Combined with the file name Update.js this is a near-zero-FP file-write signature. Cross-checked against: • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240 • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1010/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/
ATT&CKT1027.009 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal red-team simulation of UNC1151 IOCs
  • Threat intel detonation labs writing the IOC to disk
  • Backup software restoring an archived Update.js artifact
  • Security researcher repository clone containing this sample
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName =~ "system")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Hash the file (SHA-1/256) and compare to ESET's published B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC and E15ABEE1CFDE8BE7D87C7C0B510450BAD6BC0906; pull the parent process tree (expect wscript.exe with --update arg). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host via Defender Live Response or Falcon Network Containment; kill any wscript.exe/cscript.exe running Update.js; remove the WinDataScope folder and any scheduled tasks referencing it. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep org for additional WinDataScope folders, any DNS lookups to needbinding.icu / nebao.icu / algsat.icu / sardk.icu / alexavegas.icu / lavanille.buzz, and ViberPC.dll image loads.

| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where EventType =~ "FileCreated" or EventType =~ "FileModified"

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath,

| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FrostyNeighbor PicassoLoader Drop to WinDataScope AppData Folder
id: 7d83e1b4-3c2f-4d09-9f56-0b1a4f6e02d1
description: Detects JavaScript file Update.js being written under %AppData%\Roaming\WinDataScope, the fixed staging path used by FrostyNeighbor (Ghostwriter/UNC1151) PicassoLoader in the March 2026 Ukrtelecom lure campaign documented by ESET.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/frostyneighbor-fresh-mischief-digital-shenanigans/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/19
tags:
  - attack.t1027.009
  - attack.t1036.005
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains: '\AppData\Roaming\WinDataScope\'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\Update.js'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - No known legitimate software uses this folder name
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\\WinDataScope\\Update.js OR @TargetFilename:*\\windatascope\\update.js OR @TargetFilename:*\\WINDATASCOPE\\UPDATE.JS)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\\AppData\\Roaming\\WinDataScope\\Update\.js$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as process_name values(Filesystem.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="Update.js" Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\Roaming\\WinDataScope\\*" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as process_name values(Filesystem.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="Update.js" Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\Roaming\\WinDataScope\\*" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
FrostyNeighbor JS dropper self-relaunch with --update flag AIExploitation High
Detects the FrostyNeighbor first-stage JavaScript dropper's documented self-relaunch pattern: wscript.exe / cscript.exe executes a .js file with the literal '--update' argument so the second branch of the script can install PicassoLoader. The flag string is bespoke to this campaign and is not used by legitimate Windows Script Host workflows. Rationale: The article explicitly states the first-stage script re-executes itself with the --update flag to branch into the PicassoLoader drop. The double-dash --update form is uncommon in WSH-launched JavaScript and pairs with a .js argument that is rarely seen in benign workflows. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Bespoke Windows updater wrappers some sysadmins build using JScript
  • Vendor installers that pass --update to a side-by-side wscript helper
  • RMM tooling using JS-based updater payloads
  • Penetration test simulations referencing the same TTP
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"C:\Program Files\",@"C:\Program Files (x86)\") and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "explorer.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Resolve the full .js path from ProcessCommandLine — confirm whether it sits in a user-writable directory (Desktop, Downloads, Temp, %AppData%) which is the FrostyNeighbor pattern. Hash the .js and compare to ESET's published 8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F. Step 2 (contain): Kill the wscript/cscript process tree; quarantine the .js; isolate host. Step 3 (hunt): Look for the parent process — the original execution should be either explorer.exe (manual double-click) or winrar.exe/7z.exe extracting from 53_7.03.2026_R.rar. Also hunt for the WinDataScope drop and outbound DNS to needbinding.icu / nebao.icu.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--update"
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--update" and ActingProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FrostyNeighbor C2 callout to needbinding/nebao/algsat/sardk/alexavegas/lavanille AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS or HTTP egress to the six FrostyNeighbor C2 domains published by ESET in May 2026 (PicassoLoader on five .icu hosts plus a .buzz Cobalt Strike host). All six share the same actor infrastructure cluster registered between 2026-03-10 and 2026-04-14. Rationale: ESET published the full domain list in Table 2 of the article alongside first-seen dates from a freshly-registered actor infrastructure cluster (.icu/.buzz, no legitimate corporate use). Any host in a UA/PL/LT/EE government estate touching these domains is high-fidelity actor traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1010/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DFIR team detonating samples in a connected analysis VM
  • Threat-intel ingestion proxies fetching the same samples
  • Researcher accessing the article and clicking through to defang links
  • Honeypot connecting to the C2 to fingerprint it
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Defender\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the contacting process via InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName — for wscript.exe/cscript.exe parents this is almost certainly PicassoLoader. Capture the User-Agent and full URL. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole the domain at egress (block at firewall + DNS); isolate the host; pull memory and disk image. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the resolved IP — Cloudflare-fronted but the origin may rotate; check for sibling domains on the same naming pattern (*-*.needbinding.icu, attachment-storage-asset-static.needbinding.icu), and hunt for the WinDataScope drop and ViberPC.dll on every host that resolved any of the six domains.
let FrostyDomains = dynamic(["needbinding.icu","nebao.icu","algsat.icu","alexavegas.icu","sardk.icu","lavanille.buzz"]);
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (FrostyDomains)
    | extend Source="NetworkEvent"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source;
let EventHits = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where ActionType =~ "DnsQueryResponse"
    | extend QueriedDomain = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).DnsQueryString)
    | where QueriedDomain has_any (FrostyDomains)
    | extend Source="DnsQuery"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP="", RemoteUrl=QueriedDomain,
              RemotePort=tolong(0),
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessAccountName=AccountName, Source;
union NetHits, EventHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let FrostyDomains = dynamic(["needbinding.icu","nebao.icu","algsat.icu","alexavegas.icu","sardk.icu","lavanille.buzz"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImDnsActivity
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
        | where DnsQuery has_any (FrostyDomains)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Domain=DnsQuery, Source="DNS"),
    (ImWebSession
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
        | where Url has_any (FrostyDomains) or HttpHostName has_any (FrostyDomains)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Domain=coalesce(HttpHostName,Url), Source="HTTP"),
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
        | where RequestURL has_any (FrostyDomains) or DestinationHostName has_any (FrostyDomains)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=SourceHostName, SrcIpAddr=SourceIP, SrcUsername=SourceUserName, Domain=coalesce(DestinationHostName,RequestURL), Source="FW")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PicassoLoader scheduled-task creation by wscript/cscript after C2 XML fetch AIInstallation Medium
Detects FrostyNeighbor's persistence step: the JavaScript dropper downloads a scheduled-task XML template (served via the misleading Content-Type/Content-Disposition response to a .jpg URL) and then registers it. The parent-child chain of WSH spawning schtasks.exe or powershell.exe Register-ScheduledTask is article-specific. Rationale: The article describes the script downloading 'https://book-happy.needbinding[.]icu/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/1GreenAM.jpg' (which actually returns config.xml with Content-Type: application/xml) and then using it for persistence. Wscript/cscript spawning schtasks /Create /XML is a tight, low-FP pivot specific to this WSH-driven persistence pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Adobe / vendor installer JScript wrappers that schedule a maintenance task
  • Internal MDM scripts that register update tasks via JScript bootstrappers
  • Application Compatibility scripts during corporate imaging
  • RMM agents using a JScript first-stage that registers a service-task
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"C:\Program Files\",@"C:\Program Files (x86)\",@"C:\Windows\CCM\",@"C:\Windows\System32\GroupPolicy\") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Dump the scheduled-task XML (schtasks /Query /TN <task> /XML) — the FrostyNeighbor template launches %AppData%\WinDataScope\Update.js on a schedule. Capture parent process tree back to the original .js file under the user profile. Step 2 (contain): schtasks /Delete /TN <task> /F; remove the WinDataScope folder; isolate host; pull memory. Step 3 (hunt): Across the org, look for any scheduled task whose Action.Command points into %AppData%\WinDataScope or whose RegistrationInfo.Source mentions WinDataScope; cross-reference with DNS hits on the six C2 domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/Create","/XML"))
      or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ChildProcess=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          GrandparentProcess=InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where (ActingProcessName has "schtasks.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/Create","/XML"))
      or (ActingProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WSH-Initiated Scheduled Task Registration (FrostyNeighbor PicassoLoader)
id: 2c8f47a3-9b14-4ee5-b87e-91a4f5d63c11
description: Detects wscript.exe or cscript.exe spawning schtasks.exe /Create /XML or powershell Register-ScheduledTask. This is the persistence step in FrostyNeighbor's March 2026 PicassoLoader chain, in which an XML template is downloaded under a fake .jpg URL and registered as a scheduled task.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/frostyneighbor-fresh-mischief-digital-shenanigans/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/19
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1059.007

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  child_schtasks:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/Create'
      - '/XML'
  child_pwsh:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'Register-ScheduledTask'
  condition: parent and (child_schtasks or child_pwsh)
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate vendor installers that use JScript wrappers to register tasks (rare)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe OR *\\WSCRIPT.EXE OR *\\CSCRIPT.EXE)) ((@Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SchTasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*/Create* OR */XML*)) OR (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe) AND @CommandLine:*Register-ScheduledTask*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| (ImageFileName=/schtasks\.exe$/i AND regex("(/Create|/XML)", field=CommandLine))
  OR (ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i AND regex("Register-ScheduledTask", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT

FrostyNeighbor Cobalt Strike beacon ViberPC.dll image load AIInstallation Medium
Detects loading of ViberPC.dll, the final-stage Cobalt Strike beacon FrostyNeighbor masquerades as the legitimate Viber desktop messenger DLL. ESET publishes a SHA-1 (43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB) and the file is expected outside the legitimate Viber install path under the standard Cobalt Strike beacon naming pattern Win32/CobaltStrike.Beacon.S. Rationale: ESET published the exact SHA-1 (43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB) for the ViberPC.dll Cobalt Strike beacon in Table 1, classified Win32/CobaltStrike.Beacon.S. Combined with masquerading detection — ViberPC.dll loaded from a non-Viber path — this is a high-confidence final-stage beacon detection. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1010/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1055.001 T1588.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Viber portable install on a corporate device outside standard install paths
  • DFIR / red-team Cobalt Strike training exercise with renamed loader
  • Backup software restoring a snapshot containing the IOC
  • File-server hosting a software repository with the sample present
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Viber\",@"\Program Files (x86)\Viber\",@"\AppData\Local\Viber\") and SHA1 !in~ ("43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Hash-verify the loaded DLL against ESET's published SHA-1; capture the loading process (often rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe, or a sacrificial process injected by PicassoLoader). Pull memory of the loading process for beacon config extraction. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host via EDR; block hash org-wide; sinkhole nama-belakang.nebao.icu and best-seller.lavanille.buzz at egress. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts for ViberPC.dll outside the Viber install path; pivot on beacon C2 IP after extracting the malleable profile; check AAD/SigninLogs for anomalous interactive logons from any host that loaded the beacon (lateral-movement indicator).
let FrostyHashes = dynamic(["43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB"]);
let ImageLoads = DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where FileName =~ "ViberPC.dll"
    | where SHA1 in~ (FrostyHashes)
         or not (FolderPath has @"\Viber\" or FolderPath has @"\Program Files\Viber")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
              InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="ImageLoad";
let FileWrites = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where FileName =~ "ViberPC.dll"
    | where SHA1 in~ (FrostyHashes)
         or not (FolderPath has @"\Viber\" or FolderPath has @"\Program Files\Viber")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
              InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="FileWrite";
union ImageLoads, FileWrites
| order by Timestamp desc
let FrostyHashes = dynamic(["43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "ViberPC.dll"
| where TargetFileSHA1 in~ (FrostyHashes)
     or not (TargetFilePath has @"\Viber\" or TargetFilePath has @"\Program Files\Viber")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA1, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
